cards.front:
Econometrics: heteroskedasticity

Why do the usual standard errors go wrong when the error variance changes with x?
cards.back:
The formula \(\sigma^2 (X'X)^{-1}\) assumes one constant error variance.

With varying variance, the true spread of \(\hat{\beta}\) differs from that formula → the usual standard errors misstate it.

In the spending example they are usually too small, so tests reject too often.

cards.front:
Econometrics: heteroskedasticity

If the coefficients are still unbiased, why does heteroskedasticity matter?
cards.back:
We report inference, not only the estimate.

A wrong standard error can turn a noisy estimate into one that looks significant.

cards.front:
Econometrics: heteroskedasticity

Why is OLS no longer the best linear unbiased estimator under heteroskedasticity?
cards.back:
Gauss-Markov needs a constant error variance.

→ With unequal variances, a weighted estimator has smaller variance than OLS.

cards.front:
[Macro] Econometrics: heteroskedasticity tests

How does the Breusch-Pagan test detect heteroskedasticity?
cards.back:
→ Regress the squared residuals \(\hat{u}^2\) on the regressors.

→ Under homoskedasticity, \(nR^2\) from that auxiliary regression follows a chi-squared distribution with k degrees of freedom.

→ A value above the critical chi-squared rejects homoskedasticity.

cards.front:
Econometrics: heteroskedasticity tests

How does the White test differ from Breusch-Pagan?
cards.back:
It adds squares and cross-products of the regressors to the auxiliary regression.

It catches non-linear forms but spends many degrees of freedom.

cards.front:
Econometrics: robust standard errors

Keeping OLS, how does the sandwich estimator replace the variance formula?
cards.back:
→ It replaces \(\sigma^2 X'X\) in the middle by \(\sum_i \hat{u}_i^2 x_i x_i'\).

→ It is valid in large samples whatever the form of heteroskedasticity.

cards.front:
Econometrics: WLS

If \(Var(u_i \mid x_i) = \sigma^2 h(x_i)\) is known, how do you make the model homoskedastic?
cards.back:
→ Divide each observation, including the constant, by \(\sqrt{h(x_i)}\).

→ The transformed errors have constant variance, so WLS is efficient.

cards.front:
Econometrics: FGLS

What changes when the variance function h is estimated rather than known?
cards.back:
Efficiency holds only asymptotically, in large samples.

A misspecified h can hurt the estimator.

cards.front:
Econometrics: robust standard errors

Should robust standard errors always be used?
cards.back:
In large samples they cost little, so they are the default.

In small samples they can be biased downward, so HC2 and HC3 corrections are preferred.

cards.front:
Econometrics: WLS and robust errors

When exactly does WLS with an estimated variance function beat OLS with robust errors in practice?
cards.back:
Open question from class, not resolved.

A way to settle it: compare the precision of both estimates on the same data.
